name: Qiming granule (Chinese herbal formula)
short: Diabetic retinopathy trial: adverse reactions in 4 (9.8%) vs 1 (2.4%) on calcium dobesilate, none serious. Reviews: fewer or similar events vs controls; few trials report them. No dry-eye safety data.
text: No adverse-event data were found for dry eye: the abstract of a 2020 meta-analysis of 11 studies in dry eye gives no safety results and calls for more studies to confirm efficacy and safety. The data come from people with diabetic eye disease. In a multicentre randomized non-inferiority trial in 82 patients with non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy and nerve injury, adverse drug reactions occurred in 4 patients (9.76%) given the granule by mouth and 1 (2.44%) given calcium dobesilate over 24 weeks, and no serious adverse drug reactions occurred; the abstract does not say what the reactions were or whether the difference was significant. A 2024 meta-analysis of 33 randomized trials (3,042 patients with diabetic retinopathy) reported that adverse events were less frequent with the granule than in the control groups, without figures in the abstract and with mostly low-quality evidence; a 2021 meta-analysis in diabetic macular oedema found that only 3 of its 16 studies reported adverse effects. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 23 randomized trials (1,824 patients with diabetic retinopathy) found no statistically significant difference in adverse events between Chinese patent medicines, including this granule, added to calcium dobesilate and calcium dobesilate alone. In a randomized trial in which all 140 participants with diabetic retinopathy took the granule with basic treatment (half also took individually chosen Chinese herbs), there were no severe adverse effects. The cited abstracts do not list the granule's herbs. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
